title: Simply and effectively electrodepositing Bi-MWCNT-COOH composite on Cu electrode for efficient electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to produce HCOOH
abstract: Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to produce low-carbon chemicals/fuels is one of the important approaches in CO2 emission reduction and utilization. However, the insufficient catalytic activity, stability and selectivity of the electrocatalysts have been identified to be the major challenges. In this work, the novel Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalysts are prepared via a facile co-electrodeposition technique on copper foil to form the catalyst electrodes for selectively electro-catalyzing CO2 reduction to produce formic acid (HCOOH). Such catalyst electrodes show rather high catalytic activity, stability and selectivity toward the production of HCOOH. The faradaic efficiency for HCOOH production can reach up to 91.7 % at −0.76 V vs. RHE, and no obvious decrease can be observed after 12 h of continuous electrolysis. Such an electrodeposition technique to produce composite catalyst electrodes with operation simplicity, rapidity, and cost-effectiveness, exhibits a good prospect for scaled-up industrial applications.

Bismuth Multi-Walled carbon nanotube Electrodeposition Electrocatalyst CO2 reduction
A B S T R A C T
Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to produce low-carbon chemicals/fuels is one of the important approaches in CO2 emission reduction and utilization. However, the insufficient catalytic activity, stability and selectivity of the electrocatalysts have been identified to be the major challenges. In this work, the novel Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalysts are prepared via a facile co-electrodeposition technique on copper foil to form the catalyst electrodes for selectively electro-catalyzing CO2 reduction to produce formic acid (HCOOH). Such catalyst electrodes show rather high catalytic activity, stability and selectivity toward the production of HCOOH. The faradaic efficiency for HCOOH production can reach up to 91.7 % at −0.76 V vs. RHE, and no obvious decrease can be observed after 12 h of continuous electrolysis. Such an electrodeposition technique to produce composite catalyst electrodes with operation simplicity, rapidity, and cost-effectiveness, exhibits a good prospect for scaled-up industrial applications.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
With the high demand of energy from industrial production and human activity, the rapid consumption of fossil fuels is becoming concerns in terms of both energy and environment sustainability [1,2]. Regarding the energy issue, exploring new energy sources, such as solar, wind, and so on, and their associated technologies for energy storage and conversion such as electrochemical batteries [3–5]. has become necessary. Regarding the environment issue, reducing emission of CO2 and other pollution substances should be given a large effort [6]. Regarding CO2 emission reduction, there are basically two ways: one is to capture and store CO2, and the other is to convert CO2 to useful lowcarbon chemicals/fuels [1]. Compared to other technologies, the electrochemical CO2 reduction has some advantages such as utilization of renewable energy (solar and wind electricity) and abandon electricity to produce useful chemicals/fuels, and simultaneous mitigation of energy supply-associated issue and the CO2-caused environmental impact [7–9].
The products of electrochemical CO2 reduction may be CO, [8,10,11] HCOOH [12–17], CH4 [18], CH3OH, [19] and C2H4 [20]. Depending on the type of electrocatalysts used, different products can be obtained. Normally, both CO and HCOOH are two of the most
common ones, which have received more extensive research interests than others. In an electroreduction system, CO2 reduction is mainly promoted by electrocatalysts on the cathodes [21]. The frequently reported electrocatalysts are single metals, [22,23] alloys [10,16,24], metal oxides [25–27], organometallic complexes [28–30], and etc. Recently, bismuth (Bi) has been attracting more and more attention since it is a non-toxic and non-precious metal, and the CO2 reduction using Bi-based electrocatalysts can have high production selectivity toward formic acid, as reported in literature [26,31–36]. Those Bibased electrocatalysts can be prepared by both the hydrothermal [31,34] and chemical synthesis methods [32]. Although some catalyst materials can be synthesized using these two methods, their drawbacks are obvious, such as time-consuming, hard-to-control, less safe, and inconvenient for mass production. Therefore, some simple, cost-effective and scale-able methods are needed for further development. In this work, we have developed a simple method to a directly fix metallic Bi on Cu foil by electrodeposition. We have also dispersed carboxylated multi-walled carbon nanotube (abbreviated as MWCNT-COOH) in the electrodeposition solution for improving both the conductivity and performance of the as-prepared electrocatalysts [34,37]. The experimental results show that the Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu electrodes obtained after 30min of electrodeposition at different current densities can give

sections.heading: 2.1. Electrode preparation
sections.text: A 0.1mm thick, 2 cm×2 cm copper foil (Shanghai Titan Scientific Co., Ltd. China) was used as the electrode catalyst support. Before use, it was sanded, then ultrasonically cleaned with water and ethanol, and finally sonicated in a dilute hydrochloric acid for 10min. The electrodeposition solution was prepared by adding 1.94 g of Bi(NO3)3 (Shanghai Aladdin Bio-Chem Technology Co., LTD) and 2.5mL of the concentrated nitric acid (Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd), and 10mg of MWCNT-COOH to a 200ml aqueous solution. MWCNT-COOH was obtained by heating reflux (110 °C) MWCNTs (Shanghai Titan Scientific Co., Ltd. China) in a mixture of HNO3 and H2SO4 (1:3) for 3 h. [38,39] To prepare the catalyst layer, the pretreated copper foil was used as the substrate to electrodeposit Bi/MWCNT-COOH using a constant current density applied by a regulated direct-current power supply (linear DC power (Longwei Instruments (HK) CO. Ltd, China), and the catalyst-deposited electrode obtained was washed with deionized water and then dried in an oven for use. Several electrode samples were also prepared at different electrodeposition current densities. All the experimental solutions are prepared by using deionized water and all reagents were not further purified prior to use.

sections.heading: 2.2. Characterization of Bi catalysts and MWCNT-COOH
sections.text: X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of Bi catalysts were obtained on a diffraction meter (RIGAKU 3KW D/MAX-2200 V/PC, Japan) with CuKɑ radiation. SEM images were acquired using a field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, HITACHI S-4800, Japan). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were done using a transmission electron microscope (FEI Tecnai G2F20). Formate formed in 0.5M KHCO3 solutions was quantified by using an ion chromatography (IC1820, Shanghai Sunny Hengping Scientific Instrument Co. Ltd, China). Fourier Transform Infrared Spectrometer (FT-IR, Nexus iS5, Thermo Scientific, USA) was used to make sure whether or not the treated CNTs contain carboxyl groups (Nicolet Nexus 470).

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text: The electrochemical measurements were conducted on a CHI760E electrochemical workstation (Shanghai Chenhua Instruments Co., Ltd., China) and the experiments for CO2 electroreduction products were carried out in a reactor with two compartments separated by a Nafion® 117 film (Dupont, USA). The electrochemical characterizations of the electrocatalyst behaviors were carried out by a three-electrode system using a Pt wire as the counter electrode, a Ag/AgCl electrode as the reference electrode, and the as-prepared Bi-Cu/MWCNT-COOH electrodeposited on Cu foil as the working electrode. The reported potentials were converted to the RHE reference scale using E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.209+0.0591 × рH. A 0.5M KHCO3 aqueous solution used as the electrolyte was deoxygenated by bubbling N2 (99.999 %) for 30min (pH=8.6), then CO2 gas (99.99 %) was continuously bubbled into the electrolyte from the bottom of the cathodic compartment for 30min to make a CO2-saturated solution (pH=7.3). During the measurements, CO2 was continuously bubbled into the electrolyte solution to keep CO2 saturated in the solution.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
In order to prove that the treated CNTs contain carboxyl groups, we performed Fourier infrared characterization of the MWCNTs before and after the treatment. As shown in Fig. 1(a), the peak of carbonyl group can be observed around 1680 cme1, and that of hydroxyl group is at around 3300 cme1, indicating that the treated CNTs (MWCNT-COOH) indeed contained carboxyl groups.
The XRD pattern of Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalyst sample on Cu substrate obtained by electrodeposition is shown in Fig. 1(b) together with pure Bi sample for comparison. The diffraction peaks at 27.2°, 38.0°, 39.6°, 48.7°, 56.0°, 62.2° and 64.5° can be indexed to the (012), (104), (110), (202), (024), (116) and (122) facets of the rhombohedral metal Bi (JCPDS, 44–1246) respectively. The diffraction peaks at 51.2° and 74.1° can be assigned to (200) and (220) planes of Cu. From the XRD pattern, it can be confirmed that the metal Bi has been successfully deposited on the Cu foil. It also can be seen that, compared with the XRD pattern of pure Bi, the addition of MWCNT-COOH has caused the peak of Bi(012) crystal plane weaker while the peaks of other crystal planes stronger. Besides, both copper peaks are significantly enhanced, probably induced by the porous structure of Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalyst.
The SEM images of Bi/Cu and Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalysts on Cu foil are shown in Fig. 2. It can be found that after one-hour of continuous electrodeposition, the Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalyst (Fig. 2d) exhibits a loose porous structure, but the catalyst Bi/Cu (Fig. 2c) has a
small spherical structure. Thus, the specific surface area of the catalyst of Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu is significantly larger than that of Bi/Cu catalyst. Later, the larger specific surface area of Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalyst sample will also be confirmed by the double layer capacitance measurements as shown in Fig. 4. From the TEM image shown in
Fig. 2e, it can be clearly observed that the MWCNT-COOH has been deposited on the base of copper foil along with the metal Bi. The mapping diagram also shows that Bi element is uniformly distributed on the MWCNT-COOH, indicating that metal Bi has been well dispersed on the MWCNT-COOH, and that the MWCNTs are deposited together on

sections.heading: COOH.
sections.text:
Cu foil during the electrodeposition process. In this study, to evaluate the electrochemical performance of Bi-
MWCNT-COOH/Cu in CO2 reduction, the measurements by cyclic voltammetry (CV) of the catalysts were conducted in both N2- and CO2saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solutions, respectively, at a scan rate of 50mV s−1 in a potential range from 0.34 V to −0.86 V vs. RHE. As shown in Fig. 3, for both catalysts, the current densities begin to increase at about −0.8 V vs. RHE under N2 condition, which is the
indication of hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). However, the current density obtained with CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 can reach to a much higher value at the sample electrode potential than that in N2-saturated solution, demonstrating the electrocatalytic activity of Bi-MWCNTCOOH/Cu catalyst for CO2 electroreduction. A reduction current density of 26mA cm−2 at−0.86 V vs. RHE can be achieved on Bi-MWCNTCOOH/Cu (Fig. 3a), which is higher than that obtained on a pure Bi (Fig. 3b). From the chart of linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) (Fig. 3c)
and by comparing the LSV of Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu and Bi/Cu both in CO2-saturated 0.5M NaHCO3 solutions, it can be seen that Bi-MWCNTCOOH/Cu catalyst shows the most positive onset potential, which is more positive than that previously reported Bi catalysts. [40,41] These results indicate that Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu is more effective in electrocatalyzing CO2 reduction than pure Bi (catalyst), which may be attributed to the increases in both the surface area and active sites of the catalysts.
To estimate the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) of the Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalyst electrode, CVs were also recorded in the double-layer capacitance region between potentials of −0.9 V and −1.1 V vs. Ag/AgCl (−0.26 V to −0.46 V vs. RHE) at different scan rates in N2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte. As shown in Fig. 4, the capacitances are 4.53 and 0.539m F cm−2 for Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu (Fig. 4b) and Bi/Cu catalyst electrodes (Fig. 4d), respectively. The BiMWCNT-COOH/Cu has about 8 times higher capacitance value than that of Bi/Cu. This can be attributed to the higher surface roughness of Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu than that of Bi/Cu. As a result, the ECSA of BiMWCNT-COOH/Cu is greater than that of Bi/Cu, which is probably the reason for its higher performance than that of Bi/Cu in the process of catalytic reduction of CO2.
To obtain the faradaic efficiency (FE) and product selectivity of the catalyzed CO2 reduction by Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu, electrolysis was carried out at three different potentials (−0.66, −0.76, and −0.86 V vs. NHE) in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution, and the obtained results are shown in Fig. 5. From Fig. 5a, it can be seen that the electrolysis current density is increased with decreasing the electrolysis potential from −0.66 to−0.86 V. Moreover, with decreasing potential,
the FE for producing HCOOH is increased. At a potential of −0.76 V (vs. RHE), the FE for producing HCOOH is reached to as high as 91.7 % (Fig. 5b).
For preparing electrode catalyst layer, different current densities of the electrodeposition were carried out by fixing the deposition time at 30min, and then the formed catalyst electrodes were tested for electrochemical CO2 reduction. Fig. 6a shows the FEs of CO2 reduction by different catalyst electrodes (Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu and Bi/Cu) as a function of the electrodeposition current density. It can be seen that the highest FE of 91.7 % for producing HCOOH can be obtained by the catalyst electrodeposited at 7.5 mA cm−2, which is also higher than that of Bi catalyst. Moreover, For stability test of the catalyst, an continuous electrolysis for 12 h in 0.5M KHCO3 was carried out by sampling the electrolyte solution for every two hours during the test to analyzing the HCOOH contents. Fig. 6b shows that during the 12 h of the catalytic process, the FE of producing HCOOH is not significantly decreased and the current density (6∼7mA cm−2) has hardly been changed when using Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu electrode for CO2 reduction. This result indicates that Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalyst electrode prepared by electrodeposition has a high stability in the process of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction.
In general, due to different types of catalysts and electrolytes used, there are different mechanisms for the catalyzed CO2 reduction to HCOOH. The commonly accepted one is that CO2 reduction involves an initial electron transfer step from the working electrode to the adsorbed CO2 molecules (CO2(ad)) to form %CO2− anionic radicals. [42] The mechanistic pathways for CO2 reduction to HCOOH can be proposed as follows:
CO2(g) → CO2(ad) (1)
CO2(ad) + e− → %CO2(ad)− (2)
%CO2(ad)− + H+ → %COOH(ad) (3)
%COOH(ad) + e− + H+ → HCOOH(l) (4)
To further explore the kinetics of CO2 reduction, Tafel plot data for CO2 reduction to HCOOH on Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu and Bi/Cu were measured and compared, and the results obtained are shown in Fig. 6c and d. It is expected that the slope of the Tafel plot is ∼120mV dec−1
(25 °C, 1.0 atm) if the reaction with a single electron transfer to form %CO2− as the rate-determining step. [40,43] The Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalyst electrode exhibits approximately a Tafel slope of 140mV dec−1 for HCOOH, which is much closer to 118mV dec−1, than pure Bi/Cu, which has a nearly 182mV dec−1. This result suggests that the mechanism of the catalyzed CO2 reduction by Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu probably involves the rate-determining step of the first electron transfer to form %CO2(ad)− as shown by Eq. (2) [42,44]. It is easy to understand that both high conductivity and catalyst/electrode surface will favor the electron transfer. As described before, (co-)electrodepositing MWCNTs together with Sn2+ on Cu electrode really has increased not only the electrical conductivity of catalysts but also the specific surface.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text: In this study, the Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu electrodes are prepared by electrodepositing Bi and MWCNT-COOH layers on Cu foil substrate. The method shows to be simple, cost-effective, and easy to scale-up. The asprepared Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu catalyst electrode is investigated for CO2 reduction in 0.5M KHCO3 aqueous solution, and the results show that this catalyst electrode can selectively convert CO2 to HCOOH with high faradaic efficiency (FE). When using this Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu electrode prepared by electrodeposition for 30min and 7.5mA cm−2, the FE for producing HCOOH can reach up to 91.7 % at the electrolysis potential of −0.76 V vs. RHE. Furthermore, the catalyst shows to be stable during 12 h of continuous electrolysis without significant change of FE and current density. Therefore, this Bi-MWCNT-COOH/Cu is confirmed to be a potential catalyst electrode for CO2 reduction with high activity, stability and selectivity.
